accepted_candidates.title: Derivation: why a Poisson count has variance equal to its mean
accepted_candidates.visible_premise: Constant-rate Poisson law and lambda=r*Delta t, with dimensionless expected count.
accepted_candidates.visible_result: E[K]=lambda and Var(K)=lambda, immediately before the fold.
accepted_candidates.visible_conditions: Constant rate, stated count interval and distribution.
accepted_candidates.hidden_exact_span:
The variance follows directly from the first two factorial moments. Summing $k\Pr(K=k)$ gives $\lambda$. Likewise, summing $k(k-1)\Pr(K=k)$ gives $\lambda^2$. Since $K^2=K(K-1)+K$,

$$
\mathbb E[K^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(K)=\mathbb E[K^2]-\mathbb E[K]^2=\lambda.
$$
accepted_candidates.later_uses: Relative standard deviation, silent-cell example and pooled population counts; Chapter 2 uses conditional Poisson covariance.
accepted_candidates.closed_path: All uses need the visible distribution and moments, not the factorial-moment proof. No definitions, figures, IDs or typed blocks enter the fold.

accepted_candidates.title: Derivation: from random increments to the memory density equation
accepted_candidates.visible_premise: p(theta,t) is a trial density initialized at Theta; Itô evaluates the noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment.
accepted_candidates.visible_result: The zero-drift Fokker Planck equation and point-mass initial condition precede the proof, followed by Gaussian line and wrapped-ring interpretations.
accepted_candidates.visible_conditions: Zero-drift diffusion approximation, constant D and unbounded line for the Gaussian; the ring wrapping and error convention remain visible. The variable-D moment paragraph separately retains its vanishing-boundary-term condition.
accepted_candidates.hidden_exact_span:
To pass from random increments to a density equation, choose any smooth function $F(\theta)$. In a short interval $dt$, the zero-drift Itô increment has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment $2D(\theta)dt$. Taylor expansion at the starting coordinate gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[F(\theta+d\theta)-F(\theta)\mid\theta]
&=F'(\theta)\mathbb E[d\theta\mid\theta]
+\tfrac12F''(\theta)\mathbb E[(d\theta)^2\mid\theta]+o(dt)\\
&=D(\theta)F''(\theta)dt+o(dt).
\end{aligned}
$$

The higher-order terms vanish faster than $dt$ in this diffusion approximation. Averaging over the starting-coordinate density and dividing by $dt$ gives

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\int F(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta
=\int F''(\theta)D(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta.
$$

Take $F$ to vanish outside an interior region, or use boundaries for which the integration terms vanish. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives from $F$ onto the product $Dp$. Because the resulting identity holds for every such smooth $F$, it gives the Fokker Planck equation shown above.
accepted_candidates.later_uses: Gaussian spreading and wrapped-ring error, then dE[theta]/dt and dVar(theta)/dt identities. Chapter 3 uses the constant-D Brownian model taught in Chapter 1.
